name: Anarcho-Pacifism
summary: Anarcho-pacifists hold that the state is organised violence and that violence cannot be the means of abolishing it, because means shape ends. They look to nonviolent direct action, civil disobedience, refusal of military service and taxes that fund war, and the building of voluntary cooperative communities. Many are Christian anarchists in Tolstoy's line, and many combine this with a socialist critique of capitalism as itself violent.
scope: The tradition traced in Wikipedia's Anarcho-pacifism article and Geoffrey Ostergaard's 'Nonviolent Anarchism': Tolstoy's Christian non-resistance (The Kingdom of God Is Within You), Gandhian nonviolence, and the Dutch and Anglo-American pacifist anarchists such as Domela Nieuwenhuis, Bart de Ligt, Dorothy Day and Alex Comfort. It excludes anarchists who accept revolutionary violence and pacifists who accept the state. Many statements the tradition never addressed are answered low or neutral.

keyFigures.name: Leo Tolstoy
keyFigures.role: Christian anarchist whose non-resistance began the first large anarcho-pacifist movement

keyFigures.name: Bart de Ligt
keyFigures.role: Dutch author of The Conquest of Violence, joining Gandhian nonviolence to syndicalist direct action

keyFigures.name: Mahatma Gandhi
keyFigures.role: Popularised nonviolent resistance, influenced by Tolstoy

sources.usedFor: Overview, key figures, views on war, capitalism, religion and revolution.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: They favour syndicalist, cooperative and village economies and criticise capitalism as systematically violent, though they do not centre planning versus markets.

public-ownership.rationale: State ownership means state power; Ostergaard's nonviolent anarchists prefer worker-run industry and cooperatives to nationalisation.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: They reject the state's coercive taxation (Tolstoy and war-tax resisters refuse to pay), yet oppose concentrated wealth; the sources leave tax policy open.

unions-good.rationale: De Ligt and others joined Gandhian nonviolence to syndicalist direct action, so workers' organisation and the general strike are valued tools.

property-fundamental.rationale: Tolstoy held that a man may justly consume only what his own labour has gained and cited Christian objection to being a landowner; Ostergaard's strand favours collective and voluntary landholding.

worker-ownership.rationale: Ostergaard notes syndicalist-style worker ownership and management of industry and counter-institutions such as co-ops among nonviolent anarchist goals.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Surveillance is state coercion; the strand holds that the state is the active promoter of disorder and refuses cooperation with its demands.

strong-leader.rationale: Anarcho-pacifism rejects rulers altogether; Tolstoy argued that the good cannot seize power or keep it, and that rulers tend to be the worst.

state-harmful.rationale: Anarcho-pacifists call the state organised violence; Tolstoy held it inherently violent, and Ostergaard calls the nation state the active promoter of disorder.

empower-police-military.rationale: Moved (statement review, 2026-11-11) to police-more-powers: its rationale is about police powers, and this statement now asks only about military spending.

reviewHistory.rationale: They hold that armies and police exist to enforce state violence; Tolstoy urged refusing military service and rejected force-based courts and administration.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Moved (statement review, 2026-11-11) to police-more-powers: its rationale is about police powers, and this statement now asks only about military spending.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

decide-locally.rationale: Ostergaard describes radical decentralism and Gandhian village republics as the nonviolent anarchist vision of political organisation.

rehabilitation.rationale: Tolstoy called criminal trials senseless and mentioned dealing with offenders by medical treatment, and rejected courts founded on force.

abortion-legal.rationale: Pacifist opposition to killing pulls one way and rejection of state coercion the other; the strand is split and the sources are silent.

more-religion-public.rationale: Many adherents are Christian, but they reject state churches and sanction of violence by clergy; Tolstoy said churches back armies and prisons.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Nonviolent direct action was central to the US civil rights movement the strand drew on; specific remedies are not set out.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: They reject patriotism and nation-state loyalty; Garrison's declaration, quoted by Tolstoy, says "Our country is the world".

gradual-change.rationale: They reject the state's institutions as such and favour non-cooperation and building counter-institutions, though by peaceful and often gradual means; they do not defer to established institutions.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Ostergaard looks to transnational and local ties that bypass states, not to a stronger UN, which would still be a coercive state-like body.

nation-first.rationale: Garrison's declaration in Tolstoy: no appeal to patriotism for national insult or injury; "Our country is the world, our countrymen are all mankind."

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Military intervention is war; their opposition to war and preparations for war is central, even when the aim is humanitarian.

open-borders.rationale: They hold that loyalty to nation states should be rejected and that states are objects of non-loyalty; borders are state creations.

limit-growth.rationale: Gandhian village economics and simple living point toward limits, but the sources do not take a position on growth.

revolution-justified.rationale: They accept nonviolent revolution but reject violent revolution as a route to abolishing the state; de Ligt: "the more violence, the less revolution."

experts-over-public.rationale: Tolstoy argued rulers claim wisdom they lack, and Ostergaard's strand favours participatory democracy; adherents distrust governing elites.

central-planning.rationale: A centrally planned economy needs a coercive state; the strand favours decentralism, cooperatives and village republics.

state-directs-investment.rationale: It strengthens the state and conflicts with decentralism and the view that the state is harmful.

widespread-small-property.rationale: They favour decentralised, voluntary landholding but often collective rather than private; not decisive.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: State-recognised bodies tie workers to the state; the strand's syndicalism is voluntary and non-cooperating with the state.

one-party-rule.rationale: They reject rule by any party or state; Tolstoy held that ruling is doing wrong to others and the ruling class is made of those who seized power.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: They reject all rulers; Tolstoy said kings and emperors rule on force and loathed hierarchy and state violence.

democracy-best.rationale: They reject the state's coercion even when majority-chosen, though Ostergaard's strand values participatory democracy at the local level.

workers-councils.rationale: Ostergaard notes syndicalist-style worker management, and de Ligt joined syndicalism to nonviolence, so councils are acceptable as bases for organisation.

natural-rulers.rationale: Tolstoy argued that rulers are not the best, but those who love power and seize it; anarchism denies natural rulers.

political-violence-never.rationale: Anarcho-pacifism rejects violence as a means of social change; Malatesta's removal of violence from human relations is quoted as its main plank.

war-builds-character.rationale: Anarcho-pacifists oppose war and preparations for it; Tolstoy urged refusal of military service and cited the killing in war as sin.

separate-church-state.rationale: Tolstoy attacked church sanction of armies, courts and prisons, and they reject state power over conscience; some Christian anarchists reject both institutions.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Private defence still rests on force; they oppose armed defence and force-based courts, as in Tolstoy's rejection of courts founded on force.

military-superiority.rationale: They are anti-militarist and oppose war and preparations for war.

ethnic-nation.rationale: They reject nations and nationalism; Garrison, quoted by Tolstoy, says all mankind are countrymen.

class-struggle-history.rationale: They see capitalism as violent but reject class war as violence; de Ligt held that war and army serve capital, but the means must stay non-violent.

equal-outcomes.rationale: They emphasise equality and sharing of wealth (Tolstoy on consuming only what one earns), but do not frame it as outcome equality.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Tolstoy and Gandhian ethics stress love, service and self-denial; pursuing self-interest as a moral good is foreign to them.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Religious strands stress duty, but the strand also refuses state-imposed duties; split.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Tolstoy and Gandhi were critical of industrial civilisation, but the strand is mixed (syndicalists and modern pacifists differ).

algorithmic-government.rationale: More state decision-making machinery cuts against decentralism and participation.

restore-past-order.rationale: They seek a new voluntary society, not restoration of a lost order; Tolstoy sees social order as resting on a changing public opinion.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Their commitment to means as expressive of values and to principled nonviolence rules out judging policy by results alone.

direct-action.rationale: Ostergaard calls nonviolent direct action central to nonviolent anarchism, and civil disobedience is core.

means-match-ends.rationale: Ostergaard quotes that means are never merely instrumental but expressive of values; anarcho-pacifists argue means shape the ends they produce.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Not part of the strand; Gandhian and Tolstoyan simple village or farming life is the ideal, not foraging.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Tolstoy valued manual labour by all, but the strand has no doctrine on abolition of the division of labour.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The article says anarcho-pacifists often see capitalism as violent through exploitation and dispossession; de Ligt tied war to capitalist competition.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Dictatorial power is a form of state violence, which they reject outright.

collective-farming.rationale: Practical effort centred on libertarian farming communities, but voluntary, not imposed; individual holding by users is also accepted.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: De Ligt argued that war is often economic competition by other means and that capitalism cannot be made pacifist.

taxation-theft.rationale: Tolstoy and war-tax resisters refuse to pay taxes that fund violence, though the "theft" framing is libertarian, not theirs.

harm-principle.rationale: They reject state restriction of conduct generally; a harm criterion for coercion does not capture their opposition to the state.

conscription.rationale: Tolstoy urged believers to refuse military service meekly but firmly, and draft resistance was a mark of the movement in WWII.

positive-liberty.rationale: Their socialist critique counts dispossession and economic coercion as violence, implying liberty needs material means.

media-academia-power.rationale: Not a theme; they target state and military power.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Racism is antithetical to their universal brotherhood; Garrison's "all mankind" is quoted in the Tolstoyan source.

organic-representation.rationale: They reject representation through the state, preferring direct participation and voluntary groups.

total-state.rationale: They hold the state to be harmful and its power to be coercive.

national-rebirth.rationale: They reject nationalism and see change as moral renewal of individuals.

territorial-expansion.rationale: They oppose war and the nation state; Garrison's declaration rejects patriotism.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Oaths of loyalty are rejected; Tolstoy objects to the military oath.

bound-labor.rationale: Compulsion of labour is violence; Tolstoy attacked landowning as inconsistent with Christianity.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Neither Tolstoy nor the nonviolent-anarchist literature takes up the sociology of knowledge, so no position can be derived and adherents would differ.

universal-morality.rationale: Tolstoy's non-resistance and Gandhi's nonviolence were taken as universal moral truths.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Syndicalist worker management is part of the strand; de Ligt was an anarcho-syndicalist.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Macroeconomic policy is outside what Tolstoy, de Ligt or Ostergaard discuss, so there is no basis for a stated position.

rule-by-example.rationale: Tolstoy's method is moral example and non-participation; but the statement concerns rulers' government, which they reject, so adherents see it only as a fallback.

force-without-un.rationale: They oppose using force abroad, with or without approval.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Christian anarchists reject this, while secular ones may accept it; Tolstoy rooted non-resistance in faith, so the strand tilts against.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: They reject borders and national loyalty, so reserving aid to citizens contradicts them.

class-collaboration.rationale: They hold that violence should be removed from social relations, but see capitalism as exploitative; split.

workers-nation.rationale: Their opposition to nationalism, seen in Garrison's "our country is the world" in Tolstoy, rules out organising workers along national lines.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: State-enforced segregation is coercive and contradicts their universalism.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Tolstoy held that the state serves those who seized power for their own benefit; de Ligt saw the army as suppressing workers.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Forced assimilation is coercive; they reject nationalism.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy theory incompatible with their universalist ethic.

national-mission.rationale: They reject nationalism and war; spreading a government by force is excluded.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Tolstoy held that those in power are the worst and that the good cannot seize power or retain it.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Coercive eugenics is violence against persons.

night-watchman-state.rationale: They reject any state, including a minimal one that defends and polices.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Racist social pressure contradicts their universal brotherhood.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Garrison's declaration, in Tolstoy, rests on all mankind as countrymen; nonviolent ethics holds all persons equal.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A debate internal to Marxism; the sources on nonviolent anarchism do not touch it.

restrict-conversion.rationale: It would be state compulsion in matters of conscience.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Gandhian currents favour cow protection, but through persuasion rather than law; split.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: They hold the state to be harmful and reject state-building as a revolutionary strategy.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Ostergaard follows La Boétie in holding that power rests on the cooperation of the ruled, yet anarcho-pacifists deny that consent makes state authority legitimate, so the statement cuts both ways.

population-transfer.rationale: Forced expulsion is violence against persons, which they reject on principle; the opposition to coercion by the state is central to the strand.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Force against persons is rejected on principle by nonviolence; property is not central to their formulation.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: They hold that violence and struggle degrade; cooperation and mutual aid are favoured.

separated-powers.rationale: They reject the state altogether, so divided state power is a lesser evil rather than a goal.

vanguard-party.rationale: Anarchists reject disciplined vanguards; Ostergaard notes transforming relationships rather than seizing power.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Tolstoy and Catholic Worker Christian anarchists stress service to the poor and the Gospel's priority for them.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The general strike is a central nonviolent tool for the strand.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Their analysis blames exploitation and state violence.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Their universal brotherhood, as in Garrison's declaration quoted by Tolstoy, rejects the claim that ethnic or racial mixing harms a society.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: They reject state office altogether, so how offices are filled is secondary; sortition's anti-elite flavour attracts some, but the sources are silent.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Suspension of rights for emergencies is state violence.

party-commands-army.rationale: They oppose armies altogether, so a party-commanded army is rejected as much as any other.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Binding discipline conflicts with informal, voluntary organisation and conscience.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: They favour transnational ties but reject another superstate; split.

head-commands-forces.rationale: They oppose armies and rulers; a head of state commanding forces combines both and is rejected.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Tolstoy attacked church hierarchy and its sanction of violence.

clerical-rule.rationale: Tolstoy attacked churches for sanctioning armies, courts and prisons, and they reject rule by any authority, clerical included.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: They refuse to support any belligerent but also reject using war to defeat their own government; Tolstoy: take no part in wars.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: State censorship is coercion, though Tolstoy was moralistic on art; the strand rejects enforcement.

recall-officials.rationale: Participatory democracy and distrust of rulers favour accountability.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: They oppose military alliances and war preparation.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Compulsory rule is coercive, though home ownership is not central.

people-in-arms.rationale: They oppose arms for any force, citizen or professional.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Tolstoyan colonies, Gandhian village republics and farming communities were favoured.

death-penalty.rationale: Execution is state killing; Tolstoy rejected force-based courts and criminal trials.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: State-imposed curricula are rejected, though not the topic.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Legal restriction is coercion, though Christian strands object to it morally.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Citizenship rules belong to the nation-state, which they reject; descent-based membership is also nationalistic, so they oppose it.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Conscientious objection is the mainstay of their practice, so exemptions from burdensome laws are sought.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: They hold that the state is coercive and harmful and favour voluntary change; suspending freedoms for development contradicts both.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The movement campaigned for nuclear disarmament.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Peace takes precedence over territorial claims, which are state claims.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Tolstoy's position on landed property and consumption by labour; Christian view of wealth.

collective-defense.rationale: They oppose war and military alliances, and mutual armed defence pacts commit states to war.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: They reject enlarging state power, even over churches.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: They reject heads of state as hierarchy, so a ceremonial symbol of unity is no better in principle than another ruler.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Using armed force against a region is violence and the central thing they reject; decentralism favours letting regions go.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Tolstoy treated rulers as men who seized power for their own benefit, not as sacred, and they reject ruler worship.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Their objection is to rule by coercion in general, and a ruler above law is an extreme form, which Tolstoy's critique of rulers condemns.

mixed-constitution.rationale: They reject constitutional government as such.

leader-cult.rationale: They reject rulers and glorification of the state.

land-redistribution.rationale: Tolstoyan example: landowners giving land to those who work it; but not by seizure.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: They reject nationalism and territorial claims.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Tolstoy and Christian anarchists reject state coercion in matters of conscience, and punishing apostasy would be a clear case of it.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: They reject ethnic and national identity as a basis for political union, as in Garrison's "all mankind" quoted by Tolstoy.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Tolstoy located change in moral conviction and public opinion, not economics.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: They reject coercion by majorities and courts alike.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: They reject autarkic empires; local self-sufficiency of villages is different.

moral-incentives.rationale: Tolstoy and Gandhi rely on conscience, service and example rather than material incentive.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: They reject armed revolution; de Ligt said the more violence, the less revolution.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: They oppose hierarchy and rule by birth, as in Tolstoy's critique of rulers who seize power for themselves and their retainers.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Rule by one people over another is domination and violence; they reject imperial rule on pacifist and anarchist grounds.

patriotic-education.rationale: They reject patriotism; Garrison's declaration, quoted in Tolstoy, is explicit.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Imperial ambition is war-prone and based on power, so they oppose it.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: They reject state authority; a constitution does not fit.

elective-rulers.rationale: They reject rulers however chosen; Tolstoy held that rule, even by those chosen, means imposing on others by force.

minority-veto.rationale: Consensus and individual conscience mean no binding of dissenters; Ostergaard's participatory approach and informal groups.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its own rationale argues against its value: it accepts nonviolent resistance, which the statement now covers, yet gives a negative.

reviewHistory.rationale: They counsel nonviolent resistance not removal of rulers.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its own rationale argues against its value: it accepts nonviolent resistance, which the statement now covers, yet gives a negative.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

parliament-supreme.rationale: They reject parliaments and the state as a basis for power, while seeking to transform relationships beneath it.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Tolstoy was a vegetarian but sources do not set out a position on regulated animal use, so adherents differ.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Tolstoy urged giving, but rejected privilege itself.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: They refuse participation in the state but act publicly through direct action; split.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Ostergaard follows de la Boetie: power rests on cooperation; Tolstoy said force rests on public opinion.

native-born-offices.rationale: Reserving office by birth is a nationalist rule; they reject both nationalism and public office as state power.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Demanding lost territory leads to war, which they oppose on principle; the sources reject nationalism as in Garrison's declaration.

military-guardian-role.rationale: They oppose armies altogether, and a political army role adds state violence to the army's other faults.

office-by-exam.rationale: They reject state office altogether; Tolstoy held that those who rule tend to be the worst, so examinations change little.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its value turns on whether representatives must follow binding instructions, and the statement now asks only whether voters can recall them at any time.

reviewHistory.rationale: Syndicalist and participatory approach; delegates answerable.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its value turns on whether representatives must follow binding instructions, and the statement now asks only whether voters can recall them at any time.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

land-use-tenure.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about community or state ownership of land, and the statement now asks only whether a right to hold land should end when the holder stops using it.

reviewHistory.rationale: Sarvodaya sought voluntary village landholding; Tolstoy's view of labour and land.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about community or state ownership of land, and the statement now asks only whether a right to hold land should end when the holder stops using it.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

single-official-language.rationale: Imposed language uniformity is state coercion; Tolstoy and Ostergaard's decentralism both reject compulsion.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Tolstoy and Gandhi stressed simple living; Tolstoy said one may consume only what one earns by labour.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Supplying arms to insurgents is participation in violence, which they reject whatever the cause; the strand opposes war.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Invading an allied country is war by a great power, which they oppose; they also reject bloc discipline.

democratic-peace.rationale: They doubt that states spread peace; they reject spreading democracy by force, which Ostergaard calls the nation state the promoter of disorder.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Ostergaard's strand refuses cooperation with the state's immoral demands, following Thoreau and Tolstoy.

non-intervention.rationale: They oppose military intervention but also condemn state oppression; they back nonviolent solidarity.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Conspiracy prejudice against a minority contradicts their universal brotherhood, as in Garrison's declaration in Tolstoy.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Anarchists reject state institutions; adherents mixed since Christians value marriage.

local-production.rationale: Gandhian village economy and Sarvodaya village landholding, as described by Ostergaard, favour local production for local needs.

informal-organisation.rationale: Ostergaard describes collectives and counter-institutions rather than permanent parties.

national-law-over-international.rationale: They reject state sovereignty as the highest authority, so they do not prefer national over international law; neither is a goal.

religious-nation.rationale: Defining the nation by religion fuses state and church, which Tolstoy attacked, and they reject nationalism.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: They reject hierarchy among states as well as within them, so tribute to a leading power is unacceptable.

defeat-communism.rationale: They oppose war and violence for ideological ends.

religion-illusion.rationale: Many are Christian, and Tolstoy's theory is religious; secular strands differ.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: They hold capitalism to be systematically violent through exploitation, rather than progressive, as the anarcho-pacifism article describes.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Language purism is nationalist, which they reject; compulsion is also contrary to nonviolence.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Practical efforts focused on libertarian communities, especially farming ones; Ostergaard promotes communes and co-ops.

majority-settlement.rationale: State-directed settlement to alter local populations is coercive and nationalist, so they reject it.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: They reject both state socialism and capitalism's exploitation.

historical-land-claim.rationale: Nationalist land claims lead to war; they reject patriotism and borders, as in Garrison's declaration quoted by Tolstoy.

holocaust-denial.rationale: The strand regards mass killing as the worst case of state violence, so denial of it is not part of any position they hold.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Criminal law over private conduct is coercion by the state, which they reject, though some Christian strands object to it morally.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Suppression is state violence and so the thing they most reject; Tolstoy held that public opinion, not force, changes societies.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Tolstoy attacked the church for relying on state force, and they reject coercion in matters of conscience.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Imperial exploitation is violence and domination, which they reject on pacifist and anarchist grounds.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: They reject armed resistance on principle, even against invasion; Tolstoy urged refusing to take part in wars and Gandhian nonviolence replaces armed defence.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Removing rulers by force is violence; they favour non-cooperation and moral persuasion over armed overthrow.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Ostergaard draws on New Left participatory democracy.

assisted-dying.rationale: Pacifist reverence for life and autonomy clash.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Essentialising a religion contradicts the universal brotherhood in Garrison's declaration quoted by Tolstoy.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Tolstoy rejected human authority, grounding action in God's law, while denying that political authority is divinely sanctioned.

social-market-economy.rationale: They reject both laissez-faire and state management and favour cooperative or syndicalist economy, so this state-managed middle way gets little support.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Anarcho-pacifists oppose war and preparations for it and urge refusal of military service.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: They would go beyond neutrality to disarm, but oppose joining blocs.

dynastic-succession.rationale: They reject rule and hereditary privilege; Tolstoy criticised those who hold power for their own and their retainers' benefit.

property-franchise.rationale: Limiting the vote by wealth is class rule by the state, which they reject, though they do not centre voting at all.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: They reject state law as coercion, so a rule-of-law ideal is not their concern, but arbitrary decree is also state violence.

racial-franchise.rationale: Racial exclusion contradicts universal brotherhood, and they reject state franchise anyway.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: It is state coercion in private life, which they reject; Tolstoy rejected church-state enforcement.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Targeted hostility toward a group contradicts their ethic of non-hatred; the boycott of a minority is not the nonviolent economic action they use.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Tolstoy reinterpreted Christianity radically, but the sources give no general position on doctrine.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: They criticise concentrated power and wealth.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: They oppose armed forces altogether, so access to them is not a goal, though they oppose discrimination.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: State promotion of any belief is coercion, so they reject it, as they reject state churches.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Mutual aid and voluntary giving; Tolstoy and Catholic Worker.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Drilled, uniformed youth organisations train for war and national service, which they oppose as part of anti-militarism.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: The movement campaigned for nuclear disarmament.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Tolstoy: a man may justly consume only what his own labour has gained.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Tolstoy's non-resistance to evil by force, as set out in The Kingdom of God Is Within You, rules out armed defence and underlies the tradition.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Tolstoy condemns patriotism and glorifying those killed in the state's wars, so honouring them as martyrs conflicts with the tradition.

independent-unions.rationale: Anarcho-pacifists such as de Ligt join nonviolent direct action to syndicalism, in which workers' own organisations act against the state rather than under it.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The tradition's socialist strand looks to workers' own participatory control rather than state ownership, so state ownership alone would not count as socialism.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Ostergaard describes decentralist federation in which local bodies decide and delegates only coordinate.

person-over-state.rationale: Tolstoy and Ostergaard hold that the individual conscience outranks the state, and that no person may be coerced or killed for the state's ends.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Tolstoy's non-resistance rests on a spiritual and moral view of human nature, and many anarcho-pacifists are religious.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Tolstoy rejects patriotism and divisions between peoples as tools of state violence, and the tradition stresses common humanity.

racial-pride.rationale: Tolstoy treats patriotic and group pride as a cause of hatred and war, so racial pride would be rejected.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Anarcho-pacifists refuse military service altogether, including for defence, so a state army even for defence is not accepted.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Anarcho-pacifists reject nationalism as a source of war and the state; Tolstoy condemns patriotism as the root of organised violence.

communal-electorates.rationale: They reject participation in electoral politics as taking part in state violence, so they would not support separate electorates.

pollution-taxes.rationale: The tradition never addressed it; they oppose state coercion, yet many socialist-leaning adherents accept making polluters pay.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Tolstoy's Kingdom of God Is Within You makes refusal of military service the central practice, and anarcho-pacifists follow him.

sacred-nation.rationale: Tolstoy rejects patriotism and the nation-state as sources of violence, and the tradition follows him.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Refusal of violence is central; Tolstoy and Ostergaard's nonviolent anarchists reject all arms and military power, so retaining nuclear weapons is refused.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Freedom and voluntary action are central, and they reject coercive priority; they would persuade rather than compel.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: Anarcho-pacifists reject punishment by the state, and Tolstoy denounces courts and state violence; fixed sentences are rejected.

premarital-sex.rationale: Tolstoyan Christians are ascetic while Comfort and others were sexual libertarians; the sources do not settle it.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Anarcho-pacifists reject all states and refuse to take part in war, including defence of a state economy; the state is organised violence in any form.

national-church-status.rationale: Tolstoy attacked the established church as allied with the state and violence, and the tradition rejects state privilege.

equal-conscription.rationale: Anarcho-pacifists oppose all conscription and military service, so the 'or neither' option is their position and men-only conscription is rejected.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Anarcho-pacifists reject killing in any circumstance, including by the state.

self-ownership.rationale: The tradition is not framed around self-ownership; adherents split between individual conscience and communal cooperation.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: In Tolstoy's line, law backed by violence has no claim on conscience, and the believer obeys moral law over state law.

automate-paid-work.rationale: The tradition does not address automation; mutual-aid and cooperative ideals point both ways.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Tolstoy and the anarcho-pacifist tradition condemn patriotism as a source of war and state loyalty, so linking it to workers' politics is rejected.

material-over-identity.rationale: The tradition's concern is violence and the state, not left strategy on identity; adherents are split.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Anarchists reject party rule and the state, and pacifists reject the coercion on which it rests.

police-more-powers.rationale: They hold that armies and police exist to enforce state violence; Tolstoy urged refusing military service and rejected force-based courts and administration. (Moved from empower-police-military, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about military spending alone.)

former-empire-equal-treatment.rationale: Imperial ambition is war-prone and based on power, so they oppose it. (Carried over from former-empire-influence, "A country should cultivate political and cultural influence in regions once ruled by its predecessor empire.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: Citizens may rightly refuse to pay taxes that fund war and the military.
missingStatements.rationale: Tolstoy's source quotes Ballou that a Christian ought not voluntarily pay taxes, and the Wikipedia article notes war tax resistance as an anarcho-pacifist practice.
missingStatements.declined: Narrow practice that follows from the wider rejection of state and war already captured by state-harmful and political-violence-never; keeping the bank lean.

missingStatements.text: It is wrong to kill another person even in self-defence or in defence of others.
missingStatements.rationale: Tolstoy's non-resistance to evil by force, as set out in The Kingdom of God Is Within You, rules out armed defence and underlies the tradition.

notes: Most anarcho-pacifist positions on economics, family and culture are inferred, since the tradition is defined by method (nonviolence) and the state, not a full programme. Thoreau and some syndicalists accepted armed defence of revolution, which this profile excludes.
